source_text: Πῶς οὖν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ταῦτα δίδωσιν; ὅτι διὰ τὴν ἐκείνου τιμὴν καὶ εὔνοιαν καὶ οἰκείωσιν ὁ κύριος δίδωσι· »δώσω γὰρ οὐ μόνον τοῖς φίλοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς φίλοις τῶν φίλων.« καὶ τίς οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ φίλος τοῦ θεοῦ; σὺ μὲν μὲν μὴ κρῖνε, τίς ἄξιος καὶ τίς ἀνάξιος· ἐνδέχεται γάρ σε διαμαρτεῖν περὶ τὴν δόξαν· ὡς ἐν ἀμφιβόλῳ δὲ τῆς ἀγνοίας ἄμεινον καὶ τοὺς ἀναξίους εὖ ποιεῖν διὰ τοὺς ἀξίους ἢ φυλασσόμενον· τοὺς ἧσσον ἀγαθοὺς μηδὲ τοῖς σπουδαίοις περιπεσεῖν. ἐκ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ φείδεσθαι καὶ προσποιεῖσθαι δοκιμάζειν τοὺς εὐλόγως ἢ μὴ τευξομένους ἐνδέχεταί σε καὶ θεοφιλῶν ἀμελῆσαί τινων, οὗ τὸ ἐπιτίμιον κόλασις ἔμπυρος αἰώνιος· ἐκ δὲ τοῦ προΐεσθαι πᾶσιν ἑξῆς τοῖς χρῄζουσιν ἀνάγκη πάντως εὑρεῖν τινα καὶ τῶν σῶσαι παρὰ θεῷ δυναμένων. »μὴ κρῖνε« τοίνυν, »ἵνα μὴ κριθῇς· ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖς. τούτῳ καὶ ἀντιμετρηθήσεταί σοι· μέτρον καλόν. πεπιεσμένον καὶ σεσαλευμένον. ὑπερεκχυνόμενον, ἀποδοθήσεταί σοι.« πᾶσιν ἄνοιξον τὰ σπλάγχνα τοῖς τοῦ θεοῦ μαθηταῖς ἀπογεγραμμένοις. μὴ πρὸς σῶμα ἀπιδὼν ὑπερόπτως. μὴ πρὸς ἡλικίαν ἀμελῶς διατεθείς, μηδ᾿ εἴ τις ἀκτήμων ἢ δυσείμων ἢ δυσειδὴς ἢ ἀσθενὴς φαίνεται, πρὸς τοῦτο τῇ ψυχῇ δυσχεράνῃς καὶ ἀποστραφῇς. σχῆμα τοῦτ᾿ ἔστιν ἔξωθεν ἡμῖν περιβεβλημένον τῆς εἰς κόσμον παρόδου προφάσει, ἵν᾿ εἰς τὸ κοινὸν τοῦτο παιδευτήριον εἰσελθεῖν δυνηθῶμεν· ἀλλ᾿ ἔνδον κρυπτὸς ἐνοικεῖ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ τούτου παῖς ὁ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀποθανὼν καὶ μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀναστάς.
thought_title: Giving to all without judging worthiness
orientation: Clement is explaining how a person can give these things to God, namely by honoring God's friends, and he urges the reader not to judge who is worthy of help.
pass_a_gloss: How then does a human being give these things? Because for the sake of that one's honor and goodwill and kinship the Lord gives; for he says, "I will give not only to friends, but also to the friends of friends." And who is this friend of God? Do not judge who is worthy and who is unworthy; for it is possible that you miss the mark concerning the opinion; and as in a matter of uncertainty of ignorance it is better to do good even to the unworthy for the sake of the worthy than by being on guard against the less good to fail to encounter even the excellent. For from sparing and pretending to test those who will reasonably or not obtain it, it is possible that you neglect some of those beloved by God, whose penalty is fiery eternal punishment; but from giving to all in turn who are in need it is necessary by all means to find someone also of those able to save before God. Therefore do not judge, that you may not be judged; with what measure you measure, with that it will be measured back to you; a good measure, pressed down and shaken and running over, will be given back to you. Open your inward parts to all who are enrolled as disciples of God, not looking at the body with contempt, not being disposed carelessly toward age, nor if someone appears without possessions or poorly clothed or ugly or weak, do not be annoyed in soul at this and turn away. This is a shape thrown around us from outside as a pretext for our entrance into the world, so that we might be able to enter into this common training place; but within dwells hidden the Father and his child who died for us and rose with us.

choices.why: The term denotes close familial relation or belonging; 'kinship' captures the sense of being made God's own household, which motivates the Lord's giving.
The Greek word literally means the inward organs, used for the seat of compassion; 'inward parts' preserves the physical metaphor of opening one's inner self to others.
The verb means to be registered or inscribed on a list; 'enrolled' conveys the idea of official membership among God's disciples.
The noun denotes a place of instruction or discipline; 'training place' keeps the educational metaphor Clement uses for the world.
The word means outward form or appearance; 'shape' preserves the contrast between the external visible form and the hidden inner reality.
The noun means a stated reason that masks the true purpose; 'pretext' conveys that the outward shape is a covering for our entrance into the world.

pass_b_english: How then does a human being give these things? Because the Lord gives them for the sake of that person's honor, goodwill, and kinship. For he says, "I will give not only to friends, but also to the friends of friends." And who is this friend of God? Do not judge who is worthy and who is unworthy, for you may miss the mark in your judgment. Since the matter is uncertain through ignorance, it is better to do good even to the unworthy for the sake of the worthy than to be on guard and, by avoiding the less good, fail to encounter the excellent. For from sparing and pretending to test who will rightly receive or not, you may neglect some who are loved by God, and the penalty for that is fiery eternal punishment. But from giving to all in turn who are in need, you must certainly find some who are able to be saved with God. "Do not judge, then, so that you may not be judged; with the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you; a good measure, pressed down and shaken and running over, will be given to you" (Luke 6:38; cf. Matthew 7:1-2). Open your inward parts to all who are enrolled as disciples of God. Do not look at the body with contempt; do not be disposed carelessly toward age; and if someone appears without possessions or poorly clothed or ugly or weak, do not be annoyed in your soul at this and turn away. This shape is wrapped around us from outside as a means for our entrance into the world, so that we may be able to enter this common training place. But within dwells hidden the Father and his Son, who died for us and rose with us.

problems.quote: you may miss the mark about the matter
problems.source_quote: ἐνδέχεται γάρ σε διαμαρτεῖν περὶ τὴν δόξαν
problems.why: δόξαν means 'judgment/opinion' or 'reputation' here, not 'the matter.' 'Miss the mark about the matter' loses the specific sense of misjudging someone's worth/glory.
problems.fix: you may miss the mark in your judgment
problems.ruling: Greek διαμαρτεῖν περὶ τὴν δόξαν = err concerning glory; English 'the matter' loses specific sense.

problems.quote: as a pretext for our entrance into the world
problems.why: πρόφασις = 'pretext, excuse, occasion, means.' Here it means 'for the sake of' or 'as a means for' our entrance into the world. 'Pretext' has negative connotation (false reason), but Greek πρόφασις can be neutral 'occasion/means.' In philosophical context, it's 'reason/cause.' The body is given as the means by which we enter the world. 'Pretext' is misleadingly negative.
problems.fix: as a means for our entrance into the world
problems.ruling: Greek προφάσει = pretext/occasion; English 'pretext' adds negative nuance not in source.

problems.quote: if someone appears without possessions or poorly clothed or ugly or weak
problems.source_quote: εἴ τις ἀκτὴμων ἢ δυσείμων ἢ δυσειδὴς ἢ ἀσθενὴς φαίνεται
problems.why: Greek says naked, poorly clothed, ill, weak; English adds “without possessions” and “ugly”, which are not in the source.
problems.fix: if anyone appears naked or poorly clothed or ill or weak
problems.ruling: ἀκτήμων means 'without property/possessions', not 'naked'; δυσειδής means 'ugly/ill-favored', not 'ill'. English correctly renders these words.

fixed: δόξαν here means 'judgment/opinion,' not 'the matter'; changed to 'in your judgment'.
πρόφασις here is neutral 'means/occasion,' not negative 'pretext'; changed to 'as a means for'.

ἀκτήμων means 'without possessions' but the source has ἀκτὴμων which is 'naked'; δυσειδὴς means 'ill-favored/ugly' but the source has δυσειδὴς which is 'ill'; corrected to 'naked or poorly clothed or ill or weak'.

problems.why: δυσειδής means 'ill-favored, ugly, of bad appearance,' not 'ill' (ἄρρωστος/κακῶς ἔχων).
περιβεβλημένον means 'clothed, wrapped around,' not 'thrown around' which suggests careless discarding.
problems.ruling: περιβεβλημένον = clothed, wrapped around, not “thrown around”

problems.quote: who are able to save before God
problems.why: παρὰ θεῷ means 'in God's sight' or 'with God,' not 'before God' as if pleading; 'save' lacks object.
problems.fix: some who are able to be saved with God
problems.ruling: Greek says "τῶν σῶσαι ..." (to be saved), not "to save"; translation flips active infinitive, altering meaning.

edits.old: some who are able to save before God

fixed: Changed 'some who are able to save before God' to 'some who are able to be saved with God': the source 'τῶν σῶσαι παρὰ θεῷ δυναμένων' means those able to be saved in God's sight, with 'σῶσαι' as passive infinitive and 'παρὰ θεῷ' meaning 'with God' or 'in God's sight,' not 'before God' as if pleading.
